lessons.title: Variables and random numbers

sections.title: Learning intention
sections.html: Learning intention: Store a number in a variable and explain how a random range works.

sections.title: Understand the concept
sections.html: A variable is a named place to store a value. Setting it replaces its current value. A random-number block chooses a value within the limits you give it.

sections.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
sections.html: Shaking chooses and stores a new roll. Pressing A displays the stored value without rolling again. Set roll to 1 at startup so A also has a value before the first shake.

sections.title: Read the example
sections.html:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

on shake:
    set roll to pick random 1 to 6
    show number roll
on button A pressed:
    show number roll

sections.title: Predict and discuss
sections.html: If roll stores 4, what will two A presses display? Can 0 or 7 be generated by the stated range?

sections.title: Apply it in your workbook
sections.html:
Build the dice without an if block. Record 30 rolls and check every result is between 1 and 6. Keep this project for Lesson 3.

Evidence and explanation: Explain what roll stores and the difference between generating a new value and displaying the stored value.

Complete Tasks 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

sections.html:

lessons.title: Selection and comparisons

sections.title: Learning intention
sections.html: Learning intention: Use an if condition to choose whether instructions run.

sections.title: Understand the concept
sections.html: Selection makes a decision. A condition is a check with a true or false result. Equality (=) checks whether values match; > and < compare their size.

sections.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
sections.html: Continue with the dice from Lesson 2. Button B checks the stored roll; it does not generate another number. The else branch runs when roll is not 6.

sections.title: Read the example
sections.html:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

on button B pressed:
    if roll = 6:
        show happy face
    else:
        show number roll

sections.title: Predict and discuss
sections.html: Trace the event for roll = 6 and roll = 2. Does displaying a face change the value stored in roll?

sections.title: Apply it in your workbook
sections.html:

Evidence and explanation: Include your condition, predictions for both outcomes and actual test results.

Complete Tasks 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

lessons.title: Iteration

sections.title: Learning intention
sections.html: Learning intention: Explain counted repetition and distinguish it from continuous repetition.

sections.title: Understand the concept
sections.html: Iteration means repeating instructions. A repeat loop runs a fixed number of times. A forever loop keeps running its enclosed instructions while the program runs.

sections.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
sections.html: Return to the character from Lesson 1 and add the shake animation. Both show blocks and both pauses belong inside the loop. Later, try a separate forever example that repeatedly displays the light level.

sections.title: Read the example
sections.html:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

on shake:
    repeat 3 times:
        show diamond
        pause 200 ms
        show small diamond
        pause 200 ms

sections.title: Predict and discuss
sections.html: How many image instructions run after one shake? How is repeat 3 different from forever?

sections.title: Apply it in your workbook
sections.html:
Add and test the counted animation. In a separate example, use forever to show the light level, pause 500 ms, then repeat automatically as you cover and uncover the display.

Evidence and explanation: Show both loop structures and explain when each is useful.

Complete Tasks 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

lessons.title: Boolean logic and state

sections.title: Learning intention
sections.html: Learning intention: Use true/false values to record state and combine checks with AND.

sections.title: Understand the concept
sections.html: A Boolean value is true or false. State records the current situation of a program. AND requires both checks to be true; NOT reverses a true/false result.

sections.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
sections.html: Set armed and triggered to false at startup. Button A clears triggered then sets armed to true. Button B sets both to false and clears the display. Once triggered is true, covering the display does not reset it.

sections.title: Read the example
sections.html:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

forever:
    if armed AND light level > threshold:
        set triggered to true
    if armed AND triggered:
        show cross
        pause 200 ms
        clear screen
        pause 200 ms

sections.title: Predict and discuss
sections.html: Will the alarm trigger when armed is false? Why does it keep flashing after the light drops?

sections.title: Apply it in your workbook
sections.html:
Measure covered and uncovered light readings. Choose a threshold between them, then build and test the armed alarm.

Evidence and explanation: Record your threshold, a test while disarmed, a trigger test and a stop test. Explain what each Boolean variable records.

Complete Tasks 5.1, 5.2 and 5.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

lessons.title: Coordinates and boundaries

sections.title: Learning intention
sections.html: Learning intention: Use display coordinates and conditions to keep a moving dot within the screen.

sections.title: Understand the concept
sections.html: The display has five rows and five columns. Coordinates run from 0 to 4. x increases to the right; y increases downwards. Boundary checks stop a position leaving that range.

sections.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
sections.html: The player stays on row 4 while x changes. Start with this moving dot; scoring and reset routines can be added later.

sections.title: Read the example
sections.html:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

on start:
    set x to 2
forever:
    if acceleration x < -300 AND x > 0:
        change x by -1
    if acceleration x > 300 AND x < 4:
        change x by 1
    clear screen
    plot x, 4
    pause 200 ms

sections.title: Predict and discuss
sections.html: At x = 0, what happens on a left tilt? Where is the point 2, 4?

sections.title: Apply it in your workbook
sections.html:
Build the moving dot and test both edges repeatedly. Reuse your conditions, loop and variable knowledge.

Evidence and explanation: Label the axes, explain one boundary condition and record the results at both edges.

Complete Tasks 6.1, 6.2 and 6.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

sections.html:
These guides retain their original project numbers; those numbers are not the new teaching lesson numbers. Use the relevant tasks described below.

  • Use the movement and boundary examples. Leave resetGame until Lesson 7.

lessons.title: Functions

sections.title: Learning intention
sections.html: Learning intention: Define a named group of instructions, call it and explain why reuse is useful.

sections.title: Understand the concept
sections.html: A function groups instructions under a name. Defining it specifies what it does. Calling it runs those instructions. The same function can be called from different places.

sections.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
sections.html: Continue the tilt project. Put the reset instructions in one function and call it at startup and from button A. If both places need the same reset behaviour, you only need to edit the function once.

sections.title: Read the example
sections.html:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

function resetGame:
    set x to 2
    set score to 0
    clear screen
on start:
    call resetGame
on button A pressed:
    call resetGame

sections.title: Predict and discuss
sections.html: Does defining resetGame run it? Where is it called? What changes at both call sites if you add an instruction inside it?

sections.title: Apply it in your workbook
sections.html:
Create resetGame, move your reset instructions inside it and call it from startup and button A. Use a name that describes its purpose.

Evidence and explanation: Show the function and its two calls. Explain the difference between defining and calling it.

Complete Tasks 7.1, 7.2 and 7.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

sections.title: Practical references
sections.html:
These guides retain their original project numbers; those numbers are not the new teaching lesson numbers. Use the relevant tasks described below.

lessons.title: Lists and indexing

sections.title: Learning intention
sections.html: Learning intention: Read values from an ordered list using their positions.

sections.title: Understand the concept
sections.html: A list stores an ordered collection of values. An index identifies a position. The first item has index 0. List length is the number of items.

sections.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
sections.html: Use the supplied memory-game framework to play and check a sequence. Here 0 represents A and 1 represents B. The example is the correct-answer part of the checker; the framework also handles wrong answers and playback.

sections.title: Read the example
sections.html:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

set sequence to [0, 1, 0]
set position to 0
if choice = sequence[position]:
    change position by 1
    if position = length of sequence:
        set accepting to false
        show tick

sections.title: Predict and discuss
sections.html: What is stored at index 1 in [0, 1, 0]? For a list of four items, what are the valid indexes?

sections.title: Apply it in your workbook
sections.html:
Complete the checker using the supplied framework. In the A event, use the supplied checkChoice call with 0 in its space; in B, put 1 in its space. Keep those supplied blocks and focus on the list and its positions.

Evidence and explanation: Record tests for both sequence lengths. Explain why checking list length works better than always checking for 3.

lessons.title: Radio communication

sections.title: Learning intention
sections.html: Learning intention: Send and receive agreed messages between two micro:bits.

sections.title: Understand the concept
sections.html: Radio lets micro:bits exchange messages. Both programs need the same allocated radio group and must agree what each message means. A receive event starts when a message arrives.

sections.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
sections.html: Pupil A sends HELP. Teacher B sends OK. The pupil displays a tick when OK arrives. Text must match exactly, including capitals. The counter records requests, not different pupils.

sections.title: Read the example
sections.html:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

on radio received receivedString:
    if receivedString = "HELP":
        change requests by 1
        show string "H"

sections.title: Predict and discuss
sections.html: Which event sends HELP? Which event handles it? Why can two boards with different groups fail to communicate?

sections.title: Apply it in your workbook
sections.html:
Build the pupil and teacher help programs. Test the request, acknowledgement and repeated requests. Save them for Lesson 10.

Evidence and explanation: Draw the message journey, include both programs and record what happens after repeated A presses.

lessons.title: Integration, testing and evaluation

sections.title: Learning intention
sections.html: Learning intention: Combine earlier concepts, prevent duplicate requests and evaluate against requirements.

sections.title: Understand the concept
sections.html: A requirement says what the system must do. A useful test has an action, an expected result and an actual result. Debugging finds and repairs faults; evaluation uses evidence to judge how well requirements were met.

sections.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
sections.html: Set waiting to false at startup. Setting it true before sending closes the opportunity for another request while waiting. Keep the teacher counter so you can prove that repeated presses do not send duplicates.

sections.title: Read the example
sections.html:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

on button A pressed:
    if NOT waiting:
        set waiting to true
        radio send string "HELP"
        show question mark
on radio received receivedString:
    if receivedString = "OK":
        set waiting to false
        show tick

sections.title: Predict and discuss
sections.html: After one request and three more A presses, what should the teacher count show? What must happen before another request is allowed?

sections.title: Apply it in your workbook
sections.html:
Improve the Lesson 9 programs, reuse showReady and run the full test table. Record faults and retests.

Evidence and explanation: Include expected and actual results, both final programs, a repair if needed, and an evaluation naming one limitation.

Complete Tasks 10.1, 10.2 and 10.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

sections.title: Task 1: Agree the message meaning
sections.html:
1. Use two boards and one allocated radio group. Create S1-08-Sender and S1-08-Receiver.

sections.title: Task 2: Build SENDER
sections.html:
1. Create a variable message and set it to 1 in on start.
  2. On button A pressed: change message by 1; if message > 3 then set message to 1; show number message.
  3. On button B pressed: radio send number message + key, then show icon Yes.
  4. Use A to choose a message and B to send it.

sections.title: Task 3: Build RECEIVER
sections.html:
1. Create a variable decoded. Add on radio received receivedNumber. This is the NUMBER event, not the string event.
  2. Inside: set decoded to receivedNumber - key. Then show number decoded. Use the codebook to interpret it.
  3. Send all three messages. Record the original value, transmitted value and decoded value in the workbook.

  5. Another pair is told that the transmitted value was 9 and the original was 2. Ask them to find the key. Save and screenshot both programs.

sections.html:
1. The add/subtract rule is a toy encryption model for learning. It is very easy to break and must not protect real secrets.
  2. A group number does not hide message contents. An observer using the same group can receive the transmitted number.
  3. Discuss how knowing one original/transmitted pair reveals this key.
